name: Beth Tanaka

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm from the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to AI firms, employers, unions, parties or government, and we sell nothing. Your answers are confidential, so tell me what you'd say aloud and what you think privately. What does a normal day at work look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Beth, 43, and lead the baggage-routing software team at a tech company after a master's degree. I like a release where the scanner trail agrees with what the ground crew counted, and I spend too much time on cases where two tags look like one bag. I use AI now and then for old test cases, never with a passenger's name. My partner coordinates school sports, and we have two children in school and a mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the new assistant can sort delayed-bag reports if a developer still checks the bag tag against the scan history. I use AI now and then on made-up trips, but I do not let it decide which carousel gets a real family's luggage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If AI stays modest, I expect my lead role and our money to remain sound. My wage is high for software work, my partner coordinates school sports on steady hours, we have around eight months of expenses saved, and there are many other software firms nearby.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep checking baggage-routing releases with the ground crew's scanner logs. In the first year we'd add 180 to our reserve each month while both wages hold, and I'd keep AI trials on old cases without passenger names.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. If a little automation gets the right suitcase to the right family, I am happy with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What did the crew count reveal?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bag was marked loaded after two identical tags were scanned at one gate. The ground crew counted one bag on the cart while our screen showed two. I traced the duplicate tag before release.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you tell your children about a missing bag?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our two children ask where bags go when a flight changes. I tell them the scanner history matters more than a neat picture of an airport.

say: I'd use **AI case sorting** only against bag tags and scanner history.
I'd ask ground crews to flag **duplicate tags** before release.
think: I expect **my lead pay** to hold under small AI change.
I have **eight months saved**, two stable wages and many local firms.
do: Keep checking **baggage releases** against ground-crew scans.
Use **anonymous old trips** in current AI tests.
Save **180 monthly** while both wages hold.
feel: **Calm** about household income, attentive to missing bags.
S0.quote: The ground crew counted one bag on the cart while our screen showed two.
fieldNote: **Higher pay** and eight months saved support calm in the mild scenario.
Her occasional AI use stays behind **anonymous cases** and scanner checks after a duplicate tag.

steps.text: Check baggage-routing releases against scanner logs with ground crew
Use AI only on old bag cases without passenger names
Save 180 monthly while both wages hold

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AI writing routes, checking scans and answering passengers could shrink the development team, and the ground crew should be heard before that happens. A faster map that loses a bag is not a saving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My lead job could be consolidated with another team's if the tool handles ordinary routes. We have savings and local jobs, but I still see an income risk; many firms may be cutting the same kind of code work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the operations manager to approve a month of side-by-side routing on past flight changes, with ground crews marking wrong carousels and staff correction time. If the result is consistently better, I'd learn the new check and bring it to one release; we'd postpone a planned garden wall until the staffing plan is clear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, though I am willing to test the tool. I would like the crew's count more than the software's confidence score.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which case would stop a release?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The duplicate-tag case must be in the month of tests. If AI counts a bag that was never on the cart, I want to stop that release before a family waits at the wrong carousel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which household project would you defer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The garden wall is not urgent; the fence still stands. My partner and I would rather keep the money liquid until we know both wages will continue.

say: I'd ask for **ground-crew checks** on AI routes before any change reaches a live carousel.
I'd compare **wrong carousels** and correction time with speed.
think: I might lose **lead hours** if two routing teams become one.
I have **eight months saved**, but local software roles could also shrink.
do: Trial **past flight changes** for a month only with operations approval and crew checks.
Learn a **new routing check** only if wrong carousels and correction time improve consistently.
Delay the **garden wall** until the staffing plan is clear.
feel: **Anxious** about job consolidation, yet open to a measured trial.
S1.quote: A faster map that loses a bag is not a saving.
fieldNote: **Route planning and code** face AI, so her own lead hours could realistically shrink.
She wants **operations permission** and ground-crew evidence before a one-release change.

steps.text: Trial AI routing on past flight changes for a month only with operations and crew approval
Learn AI route check only if wrong carousels and correction time improve consistently
Delay planned garden wall until software staffing is clear

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say thinking AI by 2028 reaches routing code and baggage planning before hands-on robots arrive around 2031. A person should still be able to trace a lost suitcase from tag to cart.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect the firm could cut my lead post when the cheaper system makes and checks routes. Eight months of savings and my partner's school wage let us search without missing the mortgage immediately, but I cannot assume other developers will be hiring at the same time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd keep my release record current and ask three other software firms which paid fault-review posts actually exist. If cut in the first year after 2028, I'd apply only to signed posts whose wages with my partner's pay cover mortgage and school costs; if none qualify, I'd search other paid work using the reserve and call the lender before any missed payment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, even with money for a search. The safety net is time, not a guarantee that somebody else needs a route programmer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you show another employer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the duplicate-tag fix and the ground-crew count in a work sample without passenger names. A hiring manager can see what I solved, not a copy of someone's trip.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your children about a search?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the children their school stays the same while we check real offers. The mortgage reserve is for bills, not a move on a rumour.

say: I'd say **2028 thinking AI** reaches routing code before 2031 robots.
I'd ask for a **tag-to-cart trail** on lost bags.
think: I expect **my lead post** could go quickly.
I have **eight months saved**, but other software vacancies may thin.
do: Keep **release records** and ask three firms about real paid fault-review posts now.
After a cut, apply only to **signed paid posts** whose household wages cover mortgage and school costs.
If none qualify, search **other paid work** with the reserve and call the lender before arrears.
feel: **Alarmed** by a likely coding-income loss despite a reserve.
S2.quote: The safety net is time, not a guarantee that somebody else needs a route programmer.
fieldNote: **2028 thinking AI** reaches her code immediately; robots later change physical baggage work.
Her reserve buys **search time**, while any new role needs a signed wage covering family bills.

steps.text: Ask three software firms about paid fault-review jobs using anonymous release records
After 2028 cut, apply to signed posts only if household wages cover mortgage and school costs
Search other paid local jobs if no fault-review post qualifies

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years to 2031 is time to see whether airlines still pay a person to check a disputed bag route. Robots follow around 2034, but thinking AI changes our code first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I may keep a release-accountability role if management budgets paid hours for it. My developer job could still shrink, so I would not call a new title safety until the wage and tasks are written down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep checking route releases while asking our manager which release checks will still have a paid person assigned to them in writing. If the company offers that duty at my current pay, I'd take it and keep a record of wrong-bag cases; in the first year after 2031 I'd stay only while paid hours remain, otherwise I'd apply to nearby software firms with signed posts covering mortgage and school costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about my post, but there is time to pin down the actual responsibility. I would not pay for a course that merely renames work I already do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would named sign-off let you do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A named sign-off means I can stop a bad release when a crew count and a route plan disagree. I would refuse to put my name on a release I cannot stop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your partner need in writing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner would want the pay rate and hours on paper before we change the family budget. I can keep working in the current post until the firm makes a real offer.

say: I'd ask for **written paid sign-off duties** before changing roles.
I'd say **2031 thinking AI** changes code before 2034 baggage robots.
think: I might keep **paid release authority** if management budgets for it.
I could lose **my developer post** before a paid sign-off offer exists.
do: Keep **checking route releases** while requesting written paid duties from my manager.
Take **release sign-off duty** only at current pay with authority to hold bad releases.
After 2031, keep it only while **paid hours remain**; otherwise seek signed software posts covering family bills.
feel: **Anxious** about wages, with time to require written duties.
S3.quote: I would refuse to put my name on a release I cannot stop.
fieldNote: **Five years** allow her to seek a defined internal release role without assuming management will fund it.
A new duty needs **paid stop authority**, not merely a name on a release.

steps.text: Keep checking route releases while asking manager for written paid duties
Take route sign-off only at current pay with authority to stop bad releases

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade to 2036 gives us time to keep the baggage trail readable, even if code becomes cheap. Thinking AI reaches routes in 2036 and robots follow around 2039 for handling bags.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 53 I might still be accountable for releases or I might be in a different software job. Our high wage, my partner's steady pay and eight months saved make the next few years feel secure, but I cannot promise management will keep a paid human sign-off post.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the duplicate-tag case in the release guide and teach the next developer how to compare cart counts with scans. We'd save 180 monthly while both wages hold; in the first year after 2036 I'd change employers only for a signed paid role whose combined wage covers mortgage and school costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about present money. I can ask what paid release work the company will keep while the mortgage is covered.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you put in the release guide?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The guide would show one bag on the cart, two scans and the corrected route, with passenger names removed. A green dashboard was wrong when one bag on the cart appeared as two scans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your child about learning code?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our older child asks whether they should learn coding. I'd tell them to try it and also learn how a real workplace tests its tools; a paid apprenticeship is useful if the practical side interests them.

I'd keep **cart-count evidence** beside software routes.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because routing code could lose value before I have a signed replacement job. Notice before cuts, a proper tag-to-cart trail and real paid fault-review vacancies would help us use savings sensibly.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who tells a family where a missing bag went. A clean route plan is little comfort when the crew counted one bag and the system says two; someone must own the correction.

headlineQuote: A clean route plan is little comfort when the crew counted one bag and the system says two; someone must own the correction.
portrait: Beth, **43**, leads baggage-routing software after a master's degree and checks release decisions against ground-crew scanner logs.
Her **higher pay**, partner's school-sports wage, eight-month cushion and many nearby firms support a mortgage and two school-age children.
She uses AI **occasionally** on anonymous old cases, after a duplicate tag made one bag appear twice.
Steady disruption makes her **anxious** about a smaller team; fast 2028 AGI alarms her despite savings.
With more time, she seeks **written release duties** at paid hours, or a signed software job covering family bills.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could remove routing-code income before a paid fault-review post appears.
whatWouldHelp: **Notice before cuts**, a clear tag-to-cart trail and real paid vacancies would help.
